description: We are Dark Aero, a multidisciplinary team competing in the 2026 NASA Space Apps Challenge under the Universal Event. Our goal is to address the challenge of identifying Earth locations that best analog permanent Moon base environments.
summary: Dark Aero helps mission planners choose where on Earth to rehearse missions to the Moon and Mars. It compares 10 Earth analog sites, such as Devon Island, the McMurdo Dry Valleys and the Atacama, with 6 Moon and Mars target sites (Shackleton Crater, Malapert Massif, Aristarchus Plateau, Jezero Crater, Arcadia Planitia, Valles Marineris) on six parameters: geology, SAR radar roughness, slope, thermal regime, aridity and subsurface ice. It ranks the sites with adjustable weights, shows how stable the ranking is across 2,000 random weightings, warns when an important parameter fails even though the overall score is high, and labels every input as curated, measured, derived, estimated or assumed. A live scan fetches real NASA POWER climate and DEM terrain data for any point on Earth.
details:
What it does. Before rovers, suits and drills fly to the Moon or Mars, they are tested at Earth analog sites. Choosing the right site is usually done by expert judgement. Dark Aero turns it into a transparent, repeatable comparison. The user picks a target base on a 3D globe, tunes six weights (or applies a mission preset: balanced science, ISRU ice mining, rover mobility or lava habitat), and sees every analog ranked on an orbital map.

What makes it trustworthy. (1) Weight robustness: the app re-ranks the sites under 2,000 random weightings so the recommendation does not depend on one slider setting. (2) Weakest-link flag: any parameter that carries at least 10% of the weight and scores below 40% raises a warning. (3) A "Why & Data" view shows which parameters cost points and the data basis of each input. (4) A Method & Limits dialog explains the formulas, the data sources and what the tool does not claim.

Example result. For the Artemis South Pole target (Shackleton Crater Rim, about 95 K mean with a 42 to 205 K day/night range), the McMurdo Dry Valleys rank first at 86.8% and are first in 71.2% of the 2,000 random weightings. Their thermal match is only 30.9%, so the tool flags it instead of hiding it. The best analog matches geology, slope and ice well, but no Earth site reproduces lunar polar cold.

Live scan. Clicking anywhere on Earth fetches NASA POWER skin temperature, day/night range and precipitation, plus a 90 m Copernicus DEM for elevation and a roughly 1 km regional slope. Geology and SAR roughness cannot be measured in the browser, so they are labelled "assumed" and "estimated", and the result is shown as a first-pass screen (for example, "3/6 parameters from live data").

Other tools. A CSA RADARSAT SAR polarimetry lab converts HH/HV backscatter and incidence angle into a roughness index and a Mini-RF CPR equivalent. A head-to-head A/B comparator, a rover traverse planner, a 60-pair comparison matrix and JSON/CSV export are included. A guided tour explains the interface in seven steps.

Limitations (stated in the app). No Earth site reproduces vacuum, radiation or low gravity (9.81 m/s2 on Earth against 1.62 on the Moon and 3.72 on Mars). The six indices of the 10 curated sites are analyst-assigned from published agency products and are not recomputed from raw rasters in the app. The hardware and rover stress numbers are illustrative heuristics. Logistics and safety are not modelled.

Built with. HTML, CSS and vanilla JavaScript, Leaflet, Chart.js and Python. The scoring maths is implemented once in JavaScript and mirrored in Python, and an automated test checks that both give identical results for all 60 target and analog pairs. The app works offline except for map tiles and the live-scan APIs.
